images.caption: Graves of Polish President-in-Exile in front of the Polish war memorial in the Commonwealth War Cemetery, Newark-on-Trent, England. The headstone of Stanisław Ostrowski is nearest the camera. Next is the headstone of August Zaleski, and behind it the headstone of Władysław Raczkiewicz. Nearest the war memorial is the ledger stone where Władysław Sikorski was buried until his remains were translated to Warsaw in 1993.

images.caption: Two old canal-side buildings that are now pubs in the English city of Nottingham. The building to the right is the back of what was the offices of the canal carriers Fellows Morton and Clayton, the front of which now houses a pub that goes by that name. The building with the prominent Fellows Morton and Clayton name painted on it was their warehouse, and now houses a pub called the Canal House. The two narrowboats 'Megan' and 'Tinkers Leen' are part of the Nottingham Narrowboat Project and are seen here moored at their home base.

images.caption:
Grimsby Dock Tower
Pevsner says "THE DOCK TOWER, 1851-2 by J.W.Wild, is the most memorable building in Grimsby, a beacon for many miles...inspired by Siena Town Hall, but the crowning minaret is oriental. It was built as part of the hydraulic system to open the lock gates and operate cranes, the first major dock to use hydraulic power for this purpose. Of red brick, 309ft tall, taller than Lincoln Cathedral, it rises in an unbroken line to the corbelled-out top, surmounted by a further section again with a corbelled-out top...".
Note that the Grimsby tower isn't a hydraulic accumulator (it's in the category because it's an important part of their history). Towers such as Grimsby achieved high pressures simply by their height, expensive though these were to construct. It was soon realised that a pressurised cistern with a heavy iron or concrete weight on it gave the same results, at much less cost.
Photo taken from the footbridge on the A180 flyover.
